sense: of an illness, an injury or a problem: grave, dangerous

terms.gloss: serious, grave, heavy (of an illness, a wound, a danger)
evidence: Cic. Cat. 1.31: hominēs aegrī morbō gravī
Liv. 21.48.4: gravis vulnere, badly wounded (Lewis & Short)
Traupman 64, 331: gravis valētūdō, a serious illness
terms.comment: Of a problem or a mistake, plain magnus often does (see major).

evidence: Cic. Off. 1.32: graviter aegrōtāre fīlius coeperit

terms.gloss: dangerous, serious (of a wound, an illness, a war)
evidence: Cic. Att. 8.2.3: perīculōsē aegrōtāns, dangerously ill (Lewis & Short)

phrases.latin: ut saepe hominēs aegrī morbō gravī, cum aestū febrīque jactantur, sī aquam gelidam biberunt, prīmō relevārī videntur, deinde multō gravius vehementiusque adflīctantur
phrases.english: as people with a serious illness, tossing in the heat of a fever, often seem relieved at first if they drink cold water, and are then struck down far more heavily and violently

phrases.latin: sī cōnstituerīs cuipiam tē advocātum in rem praesentem esse ventūrum atque interim graviter aegrōtāre fīlius coeperit, nōn sit contrā officium nōn facere quod dīxerīs
phrases.english: if you have promised someone to come and support him on the spot, and meanwhile your son falls seriously ill, it is no breach of duty not to do what you said

eris.html: Perfect subjunctive with a long ī, cōnstituerīs … dīxerīs: the condition depends on the subjunctive nōn sit, and the relative clause is drawn into it (the house rule on -erīs and -eris).
